content: 1. A survey was conducted to assess the values and preferences of healthcare workers regarding the treatment of chronic hepatitis B infection in children and adolescents. This study involved experts such as Farihah Malik, Philippa Easterbrook (WHO), Giuseppe Indolfi (University of Florence, Italy), and Simon Ling (University of Toronto, Canada). 2. Another survey was carried out to evaluate the preferences of national hepatitis program managers concerning new directions in hepatitis B care and treatment, as well as the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B virus (HBV PMTCT). This survey was led by Philippa Easterbrook, Doroux Aristide Charles Billy, and Myat Sandi Min (WHO). 3. Case studies on laboratory-based reflex testing for HBV and hepatitis D virus (HDV) were conducted by John W. Ward, Lindsey Hiebert, Jana Manning, and Neil Gupta from the Coalition for Global Hepatitis Elimination, Task Force for Global Health, USA. 4. The overall coordination of these efforts was managed by Philippa Easterbrook (WHO). 5. The WHO Guidelines Steering Committee included staff members from WHO headquarters, such as Philippa Easterbrook, Diana Faini, Olufunmilayo Lesi, Niklas Luhmann, and Myat Sandi Min, all part of the Global Hepatitis Programme within the Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis, and Sexually Transmitted Infections Programmes. Other contributors included Wole Ameyan, Nathan Ford, Robert Luo, Morkor Newman, Marco Victoria, Lara Vojnov (Treatment and Care), and Meg Doherty (Office of the Director). 6. Additional contributions were made by Martina Penazzato (Global Accelerator for Paediatric Formulations), Mark Lanigan (Regulation and Prequalification), and Shalini Desai (Immunization, Vaccines, and Biologicals). 7. Regional and country offices of WHO, as well as other United Nations organizations, also participated. Key contributors included Doroux Aristide Charles Billy (WHO Regional Office for Africa), Polin Chan (WHO Country Office in India), Catherine de Martel (International Agency for Research on Cancer), Franck Fwamba (WHO Country Office in Chad), Kiyohiko Izumi (WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific), Muhammad Jamil (WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean), Casimir Mingiedi Manzengo (WHO Regional Office for Africa), Marcelo Naveira (WHO Regional Office for Europe), Van Thi Thuy Nguyen (WHO Country Office in Vietnam), Muhammad Pasha (WHO Country Office in Pakistan), and Leandro Sereno (WHO Regional Office for the Americas). 8. Philippa Easterbrook (WHO) drafted the overall guidelines, while Sahar Bajis and Niklas Luhmann (WHO) authored the chapters on hepatitis D testing. 9. Specific chapters underwent additional review and input from experts such as Geoffrey Dusheiko (King’s College Hospital London, UK), Simon Ling (Hospital for Sick Children, Canada), Catherine de Martel (International Agency for Research on Cancer), Emmanouil Tsochatzis (UCL Institute of Liver and Digestive Health, UK), Gibril Ndow (Hepatitis Research Group, MRC Unit The Gambia at London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, UK), Maud Lemoine (Imperial College, UK), and Lewis Roberts (Mayo Clinic, USA). 10. Contributions on referencing, web annexes, and summaries of declarations of interest were provided by Myat Sandi Min and Megan Wilson-Jones. 11. The text was edited by David Breuer, and the design and layout were managed by 400 Communications. 12. Abbreviations and acronyms used in the guidelines include terms such as AFP (alpha-fetoprotein), ALT (alanine aminotransferase), APRI (aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index), ART (antiretroviral therapy), and HBV (hepatitis B virus), among others. 13. The natural history of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection includes acute HBV infection, which is diagnosed by detecting hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and IgM antibodies to hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc). Recovery is marked by the clearance of HBsAg and seroconversion to anti-HBs. 14. Chronic HBV infection is defined as the persistence of HBsAg for six months or more after acute infection. The phases of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) include the immune-tolerant phase, immune-active phase, inactive phase, and HBeAg-negative CHB (immune-escape phase). 15. Cirrhosis, an advanced stage of liver disease, is characterized by extensive hepatic fibrosis, nodularity, and disrupted liver architecture. Decompensated cirrhosis involves clinical complications such as jaundice, ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, esophageal varices, hepatic encephalopathy, sepsis, and renal failure. 16. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a primary liver cancer arising in hepatocytes and is associated with chronic HBV infection. 17. Serological markers of HBV include HBsAg, HBcAg, HBeAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBe, and total anti-HBc. These markers are used to diagnose and monitor HBV infection. 18. Occult HBV infection refers to individuals who have cleared HBsAg but remain HBV DNA-positive at very low levels. Most of these individuals are also positive for total anti-HBc. 19. Hepatitis D virus (HDV) infection can occur as a coinfection with HBV or as an HDV superinfection in individuals with established CHB. HDV superinfection often leads to chronic hepatitis D and increases the risk of rapid progression to cirrhosis and HCC. 20. Diagnostic tests for HBV include alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) to assess liver cell injury, as well as HBV DNA testing to quantify viral load. Non-invasive tests such as APRI and Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) scores are used to estimate liver fibrosis. 21. Measures of diagnostic test performance include clinical sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value. These metrics assess the accuracy of tests in identifying infection or disease. 22. Hepatitis B treatment response is defined by undetectable HBV DNA in the blood at a specific time point after treatment. Treatment failure, or primary non-response, is indicated by less than a 1 log10 IU/mL decrease in HBV DNA after three months of therapy. 23. Antiviral drug resistance can be confirmed by sequencing the HBV DNA polymerase and identifying specific genetic markers of resistance.
